summary: Children extend coordinate work to all four quadrants: plotting and reading points such as (−3,4) and (2,−5), naming which quadrant a point lies in, and reasoning about positions where either or both coordinates are negative. The new demand is reading a SIGNED scale on each axis — a negative x means left of the origin, a negative y means below it, with numbers running symmetrically outward from 0 — fused to the ordered-pair (across, then up/down) rule. Live plotting with immediate feedback lets wrong-direction and reversed placements surface and be corrected; discrete practice items and labelled grids can check and clarify but elicit less of the felt signed movement.
misconceptions: Moving the wrong way for a negative coordinate — counting right for −3 or up for −5 — through weak grasp of order on a signed scale.
Putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, placing the point in the wrong quadrant.
Mis-ordering negatives (treating −5 as further out than −3 because 5>3), so points on a negative axis are misplaced.
Counting from '1' at the origin instead of '0', landing one square off.

activities.title: Plot it as a signed journey from the origin
steps: On a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes, plot (−3,4): move LEFT 3 along the x-axis from the origin, then UP 4 along the y-axis, treating each sign as a direction.
Name the quadrant from its sign pattern: (−,+) is the second (top-left) quadrant.
Plot (2,−5) (two right, five down) and (−4,−1) (four left, one down), naming each quadrant from its two signs.

If a live tool is available, place the marker yourself and watch it replay the two signed moves; if you counted right for the −3 and landed in the (+,+) quadrant, notice the mismatch and re-plot reading the minus as 'left'.
Where offered, use a reflect-in-axis toggle to flip (−3,4)↔(3,4)↔(3,−4) and watch a single sign change hop the point across an axis.
activities.insight: A minus sign is a DIRECTION (left of, or below, the origin), not decoration on the digit; the quadrant is read directly from the pair of signs, and flipping one sign reflects the point across an axis.

activities.title: Anchor each axis as a signed number line
steps: Treat the x-axis as a horizontal number line and the y-axis as a vertical one, both meeting at 0 at the origin.
Point and chant positive and negative values along a counting stick held horizontally, then vertically, forwards and backwards, so left and below map to negatives.
Use a thermometer or below-ground/depth scale as a familiar signed vertical axis.
Count the MOVES from the origin (which is 0), not the lines including it, so you do not land one square off.
Say aloud why −3 goes three to the LEFT: the numbers mirror symmetrically outward from 0.
activities.insight: Each axis is a signed number line symmetric about 0; reading position (not the bare digit) on that scale is what fixes direction and ordering.

activities.title: Reason across quadrants and name the quadrant from the signs
steps: Without plotting, state which quadrant (−2,−7) lies in and explain how you can tell from the two signs.
Find the fourth vertex of a square given three vertices such as (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0), coordinating the signs rather than plotting in isolation.
Compare (−5,0) and (−3,0): decide which is further from the origin and justify it by position on the negative scale (five to the left versus three).
Label each quadrant by its sign pattern: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−), and connect this to reflections in the axes.
Respond to a counterexample: 'A friend plotted (−3,4) in the top-right — what would you say?' (a negative x must go left).
activities.insight: For a point with two non-zero coordinates, quadrant membership is a reading of the two signs; a point with a zero coordinate, such as (3,0), (0,3) or (−5,0), lies on an axis and is in no quadrant. Coordinating signs across quadrants and comparing negatives by distance from the origin transfers the skill beyond single plots.

activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted items
steps: Tap/draw to plot (−3,4); choose which quadrant (2,−5) is in; fill in the coordinates of a plotted point; put −5, −3, 0, 2 in order along an axis.

For multiple-choice quadrant questions, the wrong options should encode real errors — the reversed point, the same point with one sign flipped, and the point mis-ordered on the negative scale — so a wrong answer shows which misconception is present.
activities.insight: Discrete items confirm the skill and diagnose which specific error (reversal, sign-as-decoration, or mis-ordered negatives) is present.

checkQuestion: Put a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes in front of the child. Say: 'Plot these three points and label each with its coordinates: (−3, 4), (2, −5), and (−4, −1). For each one, tell me which quadrant it is in. Then look at (−5, 0) and (−3, 0) — which is further from the origin, and how do you know?' Set the task and WATCH how each point is reached from the origin; do not explain the axes.
checkAnswer: The child moves along x first then y, treating each sign as a direction — (−3,4) three left and four up (second quadrant), (2,−5) two right and five down (fourth quadrant), (−4,−1) four left and one down (third quadrant) — labels each pair as (across, up), names the quadrant from the sign pattern, and reasons that (−5,0) is further from the origin than (−3,0) because −5 is further along the negative scale (five to the left versus three).
